content.title: Modals and hedging: expressing degrees of certainty
content.instructions: Complete each sentence with a modal verb or hedging expression that matches the meaning in brackets, followed by the correct form of the verb given. For example: (possibly / rise) → may rise. Where the word in brackets is itself a modal or hedging word (would, could, tend, likely, appear), build your answer around it.

items.prompt: The rise in sales in 2015 ___ (possibly / be) the result of a successful advertising campaign, although the chart gives no reasons.
items.model_answer: The rise in sales in 2015 may have been the result of a successful advertising campaign, although the chart gives no reasons.
items.explanation: To speculate about the past, use may / might / could + have + past participle. 'Could be' or 'may be' would wrongly refer to the present.

items.prompt: The decline in newspaper sales ___ (impossible / be) due to rising prices alone, since prices barely changed during the period.
items.model_answer: The decline in newspaper sales cannot have been due to rising prices alone, since prices barely changed during the period.
items.explanation: For a confident negative deduction about the past, use can't / cannot / couldn't + have + past participle. Note that 'mustn't have been' is not used for deduction.

items.prompt: The sharp fall in visitor numbers in 2020 ___ (almost certain / cause) by travel restrictions during the pandemic.
items.model_answer: The sharp fall in visitor numbers in 2020 must have been caused by travel restrictions during the pandemic.
items.explanation: A confident positive deduction about the past uses must + have + past participle; here the passive form is needed (must have been caused). 'Was almost certainly caused' expresses the same degree of certainty with an adverb.

items.prompt: It ___ (could / argue) that free public transport would benefit low-income families most.
items.model_answer: It could be argued that free public transport would benefit low-income families most.
items.explanation: 'It could be argued that …' is a modal passive (modal + be + past participle) that introduces a view tentatively. It is ideal for presenting an opposing opinion in Task 2 before you evaluate it.

items.prompt: Rising house prices ___ (likely / discourage) young people from moving to the capital in the coming years.
items.model_answer: Rising house prices are likely to discourage young people from moving to the capital in the coming years.
items.explanation: 'Be likely to + base verb' expresses a probable future outcome and is more cautious than 'will'. Remember that 'likely' is an adjective, so it needs the verb 'be' (are likely to), not 'likely discourage'.

items.prompt: Older people ___ (tend / be) more cautious about sharing personal data online than teenagers.
items.model_answer: Older people tend to be more cautious about sharing personal data online than teenagers.
items.explanation: 'Tend to + base verb' describes a general pattern without claiming it is true of every individual. It is one of the most useful hedges for generalisations about groups in Task 2 and Speaking Part 3.

items.prompt: The government ___ (appear / underestimate) the cost of the new high-speed rail line, which is now twice the original budget.
items.model_answer: The government appears to have underestimated the cost of the new high-speed rail line, which is now twice the original budget.
items.explanation: 'Appear / seem + perfect infinitive (to have + past participle)' hedges a claim about something that happened in the past. The verb agrees with the singular subject: the government appears.

items.prompt: I ___ (would / not / say) that technology has made us lazier, but it has certainly changed our daily habits.
items.model_answer: I wouldn't say that technology has made us lazier, but it has certainly changed our daily habits.
items.explanation: 'Would' softens an opinion. 'I wouldn't say that …' sounds more polite and more natural in Speaking Part 3 than a blunt 'I don't think …' or 'That's wrong'.

items.prompt: In the future, more professionals ___ (possibly / choose) to work remotely from rural areas.
items.model_answer: In the future, more professionals may well choose to work remotely from rural areas.
items.explanation: May / might / could + base verb express future possibility. Adding 'well' (may well, might well) signals a fairly strong possibility while still hedging the prediction.

items.prompt: In my view, governments ___ (advisable / invest) far more in mental health services for young people.
items.model_answer: In my view, governments should invest far more in mental health services for young people.
items.explanation: 'Should' and 'ought to' + base verb make a recommendation. They are stronger than 'could' but less forceful than 'must', which makes them the usual choice for solutions in a Task 2 essay.
